content.text: {"relation":"MATCH","consensus_summary":"When used symbolically, fornication/whoredom denotes spiritual unfaithfulness to God — chiefly idolatry and apostasy — framed by the marriage metaphor of the covenant, with the unfaithful people portrayed as a harlot. Common subsidiary emphases include illicit political/commercial alliances with foreign powers, corrupt religion, and the Babylon imagery of Revelation; the literal sexual sense grounds the metaphor.","book_summary":"Covenant unfaithfulness — joining oneself to other gods or kingdoms outside the union God established, with the physical sin supplying the image.","consensus_core_identification":"Spiritual/covenant unfaithfulness to God, principally idolatry (worship of or attachment to other gods), with reliance on foreign powers as a closely related expression of the same infidelity, all built on the marriage metaphor.","book_core_identification":"Covenant unfaithfulness: attachment to other gods or other kingdoms outside the God-established union, with literal sexual sin as the source image.","core_relation":"EQUIVALENT","extension_relation":"SAME_CASES","boundary_disagreement":"None of substance. The book folds the political-alliance sense ('other kingdoms') into its one-line core, whereas most consensus responses list it as a common secondary emphasis; but the consensus explicitly treats alliances as an expression of the same unfaithfulness motif (e.g., Ezekiel 16 and 23, Isaiah 30–31, Revelation 17:2), so the covered cases are the same.","material_contradiction":"None.","rationale":"Both readings identify the symbol identically: covenant infidelity to God pictured through the marriage metaphor, with the literal sexual sin supplying the image (Response B's note says exactly this). The book's inclusion of 'kingdoms' alongside 'gods' mirrors the consensus's widely acknowledged political-alliance dimension, which every response lists as common or as part of the primary basis. There is no narrowing, broadening, or reclassification of cases — only compression of the consensus's primary meaning plus its most common companion sense into a single definition.","citation_support":"STRONG","strongest_objection":"One could argue the book slightly broadens the core by elevating political alliance ('kingdoms') from a secondary application to co-equal status within the core identification, which could warrant REFINED; however, since the consensus already treats alliance-whoredom as the same unfaithfulness motif (and Rev 17:2 and Ex 34:15, printed with the entry, explicitly involve kings/covenants with nations), this is a difference of emphasis, not extension.","confidence":"high"}
